video.title: Deeper Than Just "Footwork" | Tennis Movement Fundamentals Explained

classification.reason: The coach analyzes Roger Federer's footwork and movement mechanics to explain the fundamentals of wide base, triple bend, and force absorption, then provides progressive lower-body conditioning drills.

problem.title_as_question: Why do players struggle to move explosively and stay balanced on the tennis court?
problem.definition: Recreational players often move with narrow stances and straight legs, landing flatfooted and unable to generate lateral leverage or absorb force effectively.

symptoms.description: The player recovers or receives balls with feet close together and weight back on the heels.
The player lands flatfooted from the split step and is unable to push off into motion immediately.
A feeling that getting into an athletic wide stance is comically or unnaturally wide.

causes.statement: Players maintain an overly narrow stance width, restricting leg push vectors to vertical rather than lateral directions.
Players land from their split step before recognizing where the ball is travelling, resulting in a static, flatfooted landing.
Lack of a triple bend at the hips, knees, and ankles disengages the lower-body musculature and prevents force absorption and lateral pushing.
The brain subconsciously forces a narrow stance to protect unprepared soft tissues from higher physical impact forces.

angles.summary: Tennis footwork is not about rigid footstep choreography, but rather goal-oriented perception and lower-body coordination.
A narrow stance restricts leg pushing forces to up and down, whereas a wider base redirects muscular force laterally to drive movement and balance.
Roger Federer demonstrates a narrow, heel-heavy stance when thinking a shot went out, contrasted with an immediate wide, intense stance upon realizing the point continues.
Federer maintains single-foot balance when transitioning forward, avoiding full sprints so his trailing foot can hover without collapsing.

solutions.summary: Split step late enough and high enough to read the incoming ball trajectory midair and land directly into motion.
Perform fast-feet line taps by crossing one foot over and back across a line while tapping in place on the other foot to engage the triple bend.
Lift one foot slightly off the ground and practice landing into a soft triple bend to train lower-body force absorption.
Jump laterally onto one foot and freeze for a 5-second countdown to completely absorb force before leaping back.
Perform the lateral jump and hold drill with both hands placed behind the back to isolate balance strictly to the lower body.
